text:
NextItNet predicts next items through stacked causal dilated convolutions and residual connections; dilation expands the accessible history without pooling. Its autoregressive objective supports different prediction endpoints. Removing oldest interactions while keeping target x[t+1] produces suffix x[s:t] → x[t+1]: a context-length intervention with unchanged recent history and target. Sampling an earlier endpoint instead produces x[:j] → x[j+1], j<t: a different training example, recent context and usually target. Keeping x[t+1] after ending at j would introduce a prediction gap. These distinctions follow from the conditional formulation in the [NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf).

Architectural deduction: for stride-one causal convolutions, receptive-field width R = 1 + Σℓ(kℓ−1)dℓ, counting every temporal convolution, including multiple convolutions inside residual blocks. At fixed weights in deterministic evaluation, deleting only items before the final R input positions leaves the final prediction unchanged if all inputs and operations in its dependency graph remain identical. Fixed-length left padding preserves retained positions; read the final nonpadding position, not nonpadding_count−1. Cropping into the receptive field can change predictions. Reindexing absolute positional embeddings, changing boundary/padding behavior, or normalization/pooling across sequence positions can also break invariance; per-position channel normalization does not. Even when the final prediction is invariant, training can change if cropping removes auxiliary per-position losses or changes their weighting.
